
**Beyond NHI: Establishing Identity for Agentic AI Systems

The AI Identity Maturity Model (AIMM)

Authors’ Note: This is the authors' independent work, reflecting their personal views and not representing any employer or organization. It is based on publicly available open standards and open-source technologies. No confidential or proprietary information from any employer is included. This article is not legal, regulatory, compliance, or procurement advice. AIMM is a technical maturity model for agentic identity controls. It is not a compliance framework, does not assert conformance with any regulatory regime, and should not be relied on as legal or compliance advice. Organizations subject to specific regulatory requirements should map AIMM concepts to their own controls and obtain qualified advice on applicability.

AI agents are changing the identity problem.

A chatbot can give a bad answer. An agent can take an action. Agents are now trusted to read private data, call tools, modify records, trigger workflows, write code, or delegate work to another agent. It can even impersonate a legitimate user entirely — as demonstrated by CVE-2025-12420, where an unauthenticated actor could assume any user's identity through ServiceNow's AI agent API and perform all actions that user was authorized to take. Once software can act with autonomy, the key question is no longer only “Is the model safe?” It becomes: who or what is acting, under whose authority, from which environment, with what scope, and with what evidence?

That is why agentic AI security starts with identity. OWASP’s Top 10 for Agentic Applications identifies identity and privilege abuse, tool misuse, insecure inter-agent communication, cascading failures, and rogue agents as core risks for autonomous systems [1]. These are not just model-behavior challenges but rather are deployment-layer problems. When an agent is over-permissioned, compromised, misled, or mis-scoped, the identity architecture determines the blast radius. Let's take a deeper look at how agents can break us at machine speed in the next section.

# When the Agent turns Adverserial

Four failure classes appear repeatedly in production agentic systems which are depicted below.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The first looks like an NHI problem solved by tighter scoping. The other three are structurally agentic and do not exist in single-workload threat models. Add to this what [CISA Joint Advisory AA25-239A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa25-239a) documents — Chinese state-sponsored APTs systematically compromising the network backbone and harvesting authentication credentials at scale — and agents become the highest-speed lateral-movement vector in the environment. Mature identity is the structural control that addresses all four.

# NHI ≠ Agent Identity

The industry uses these interchangeably. They aren’t the same — and conflating them means spending a real budget on the wrong problem. The [OWASP NHI Top 10 (2025)](https://owasp.org/www-project-non-human-identities-top-10/2025/) catalogs the failure modes of authenticating software (secret leakage, overprivilege, long-lived keys). Those risks still matter. Agents amplify them, and add new ones.

|   |
|---|
|NHI authenticates software. Agent Identity governs autonomous action.|

A workload identity (e.g. via [SPIFFE/SPIRE](https://spiffe.io/docs/latest/spire-about/spire-concepts/) or [IETF WIMSE](https://datatracker.ietf.org/wg/wimse/documents/)) proves which software component is running. Agent identity must also decide whether this specific action, in this specific context, with this delegated authority, should be allowed — across delegations, tools, and trust domains.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

This leads to a point that has been quietly avoided: until your identity stack supports full-stack attestation, delegation-chain continuity, and context-bound authority, what you have is well-managed NHI, not Agent Identity. The threshold matters because the two solve different problems with different threat models.

The Agentic Identity Maturity Model

Maturity in agentic identity is incremental, nuanced and uneven. Most organizations are mature on some aspects of identity operations but lacking in others at the same moment. The Agentic Identity Maturity Model (AIMM) measures four pillars independently, each on a five-level assurance scale (independent of OWASP ASVS verification levels) where every level requires the levels beneath it. The pillars are Identity and Attestation, Authorization and Scoped Delegation, Traceability with Intent and Provenance, and Operational Readiness. AIMM is an assurance framework, not a vendor taxonomy or a product, and it is built around one of those four pillars rather than treating them as equals.

  

That pillar is Identity. The other three exist to support it: authorization scopes an identity, traceability attributes actions to an identity, and operational readiness contains an identity. None of them has meaning until the system can first say which agent is acting and keep confirming that the agent still deserves the trust it holds. Identity in agentic AI cannot stand alone either, which is why the supporting pillars are not optional. A workload identity proves which software is running; it does not prove that the software is acting within its authorized purpose, that its authority narrowed correctly as it delegated, or that anyone can reconstruct what it did. A correctly identified agent with inherited permissions and no audit trail is still an incident waiting to happen. Identity is necessary and insufficient, and the supporting pillars close the gap between proving who an agent is and trusting what it does.

  

|   |
|---|
|Note: Before any pillar applies, the organization has to be able to enumerate its agents, including shadow agents, tools, plugins, registries, and discovered peers. An organization that cannot yet enumerate its agents should treat discovery as the first priority before scoring against any pillar. Discovery is the precondition for governance which is covered in solutions like the OWASP’s Agent Name Service.|

  

![](data:image/png;base64,)

### Pillar 1 — Identity and Attestation (the core)

The question this pillar answers is whether an organization can cryptographically attest who every agent is, and re-verify over the life of a session that it still merits that trust. Every other pillar binds to the answer, so the model's floor is most often set here.

  

- Identity in a registry: At Level 1, agents carry unique identifiers and appear in a registry, and they authenticate with cryptographic credentials such as signed tokens or key pairs rather than plaintext secrets, shared accounts, personal access tokens, or borrowed human credentials. Trust is not granted on network location. This rejects implicit trust based only on network position or asset ownership [3], and it moves past the replay exposure of bearer secrets, where RFC 6750 notes that any holder of a bearer token can use it without proving possession of a key [4].
    
- Brokered short-lived credentials: At Level 2, each agent holds its own short-lived key-pair credential rather than a borrowed one, rotation is automated to under a day, and delegation-chain metadata travels in the token. Identity is issued to a known workload by a platform or broker. This is the maturity leap from "the agent has a key" to "a trusted system issued identity to this workload," the pattern the IETF WIMSE working group is standardizing for workload identity across heterogeneous environments [5].
    
- First-class IdP entity: At Level 3, agents become first-class entities in the identity provider. Certificate-backed composite tokens carry both the human and the agent claim, every invocation path is covered whether browser, command line, scheduled job, or API, and credentials are re-issued against current evidence rather than treated as a badge granted once at startup. Continuous attestation begins here: the relying system can ask whether the workload still matches the conditions required to act with this authority.
    
- Standards-based workload identity: At Level 4, identity rests on a recognized cryptographic workload-identity standard, for example SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Documents issued by SPIRE after node and workload attestation [6], with continuous mutual TLS, runtime re-attestation in long sessions, and key material held in hardware security modules or secure enclaves. 
    
- Full-stack attestation: At Level 5, attestation becomes full-stack and location-aware: evidence spans agent code, runtime, host, platform, and a hardware root of trust, following the IETF RATS architecture for evaluating whether a system is in an intended operating state [7] and the Entity Attestation Token format for carrying those claims [8]. Code is cryptographically bound to the credential, and coarse, privacy-preserving region claims are available where residency or sovereignty rules require them.
    

### Pillar 2 — Authorization and Scoped Delegation

Identity establishes who is acting. Authorization governs what that identity may do, and narrows it at every delegation hop. A correctly identified agent with inherited permissions is still an Excessive Agency incident waiting to happen, which is why this pillar matters even when Identity is strong.

  

- Full-stack attestation: At Level 1, agents operate under an authenticated identity with no anonymous access, and access incidents are tracked. 
    
- Explicit downscoping:At Level 2, the model shifts to default-inherit with explicit downscoping: per-agent permission boundaries, writes that require approval, permissions calibrated to data-sensitivity tiers, and separated sandbox, staging, and production environments. Token exchange swaps a human session for a scoped, short-lived agent token, the pattern defined in RFC 8693 [9].
    
- Policy-engine enforcement: At Level 3, a policy engine applies dynamic, risk-adjusted scoping, and the agent itself enforces policy across all output paths rather than trusting upstream checks. Per-request scopes are expressed through Resource Indicators [10] and Rich Authorization Requests [11], and tokens are sender-constrained through mutual-TLS binding or DPoP so a stolen token alone cannot act [12][13].
    
- Purpose-bound JIT delegation: Levels 4 and 5 carry the weight of multi-agent delegation, the hardest authorization problem agents introduce. Agents rarely act alone: a user asks an agent to do something, that agent calls a tool, exchanges a token, and delegates to another agent, and each hop can dilute context and create a confused-deputy risk. At Level 4, permissions are scoped to a declared purpose per request, provisioned just in time with automatic expiry, and gated by a rule-of-two control for critical operations. Each hop receives narrowed, recipient-bound authority, so delegation narrows scope instead of impersonating the original principal. 
    
- Cross-domain verifiable authority: At Level 5, authority boundaries become machine-verifiable across trust domains, with real-time consent verification and agent-to-agent chains whose scope continuously narrows. Authority is granted only because the current request, runtime attestation, delegation path, and policy together justify it.
    

### Pillar 3 — Traceability with Intent and Provenance

Where authorization decides what may happen, traceability proves what did happen, to a standard that holds up after the fact. The word intent here is precise and load-bearing: it means declared, attributable purpose, never a model's inner cognition. This pillar is meant to distinguish a normal NHI from a truly agentic identity. Identity systems can carry and enforce the purpose an agent was given, the authority it was delegated, and the context it ran in. They cannot read a model's mind, and treating a log as evidence of inner intent confuses the record with the reasoning. This distinction matters for accuracy, for auditability, and for privacy, because the goal is to capture what the agent was authorized to do and what it actually did, not to capture how it thought.

  

- Attributable action logs: At Level 1, access attempts are logged with timestamps and an actor identifier, agent traffic is distinguishable from human traffic, and the originating prompt or task is captured. 
    
- Purpose-bound audit trail: At Level 2, agent identity appears in every access log, every audit entry attributes the action to the human behind it, and declared-purpose context, meaning the prompt, task, or trigger that authorized the action, travels with each action in structured decision logs that map purpose to action.
    
- End-to-end delegation chain: Level 3 is where the delegation chain becomes the central concern, the trace-side counterpart to the multi-agent authority problem in Pillar 2. Session and tracer identifiers correlate actions across systems, and the full chain is traceable from the human request through every agent and tool hop to the final execution. For long-running and scheduled agents, purpose freshness is re-verified so that a stale mandate is caught before it drifts, for example when a role change silently expands an agent's reach. Non-repudiation follows ISO 13888 over immutable trails. Critically, preserving the chain does not mean exposing it: mature systems retain verifiable chain state for authorized policy, audit, and forensics while disclosing only the actor context each downstream recipient is entitled to see, a selective, need-to-know posture that is what makes multi-agent and cross-boundary traceability safe rather than a privacy liability.
    
- Real-time provenance analytics: At Level 4, behavioral analytics run in real time with anomaly detection and per-session risk scoring, third parties can verify provenance, and evidence reports can be automatically generated. 
    
- Verifiable lifecycle credentials: At Level 5, behavior is continuously attested against declared purpose, execution records are tamper-evident across the full lifecycle from creation through delegation to completion, and authority and provenance claims are expressed as W3C Verifiable Credentials [18] for machine-verifiable proof across organizational boundaries.
    

### Pillar 4 — Operational Readiness

Friction is the cost teams underweight, and it is measurable. A denied agent does not stop and ask for help. It retries, reformulates the request, and reasons around the block, and each of those moves spends tokens. Independent benchmarking of MCP-style tool calling puts the overhead of a failed call far above the call itself: in a reason-act-observe loop, a failed tool call costs not just its own tokens but the recovery reasoning, the retry, and the context bloat from the failed attempt sitting in the window, with measured token overhead reaching as high as 35x against direct tool invocation [26]. At fleet scale this stops being a rounding error. Unconstrained agent loops have been reported to exhaust API budgets within hours [27]. Add the human time spent unblocking agents whose context has already expired, and the waste is material before any breach occurs. The constraint underneath all of this is tempo: agents request access at machine speed, so an access decision that routes through a human approval queue and resolves in minutes has already failed. Identity questions have to be answered as fast as agents ask them. The north star of this pillar is reactive IAM: requesting, granting, and revoking scoped authority under policy at machine speed.

The first three pillars decide whether an action is identified, authorized, and recorded. Operational readiness decides what happens when one of them fails, and whether the identity layer scales as agent volume grows. It covers three things: containment, friction, and adaptive capacity. Containment limits the blast radius of a bad action. It runs from cataloged assets and manual revocation at Level 1, through global guardrails on privileged systems and audited, time-bounded break-glass at Level 2, to per-team guardrails and rate-limited blast-radius caps at Level 3, to automated guardrails with signal-triggered containment and pre-approved response playbooks at Level 4, to self-healing guardrails that retune on live risk signals at Level 5. Adaptive capacity measures whether the framework scales without manual work, from hand-provisioning each new agent type to auto-scaling for a tenfold jump in agent population.

### The Capability Matrix - The AIMM Matrix: Levels, Floors, and Risk

The four-by-five matrix is the working artifact of the framework, and it carries three layers at once. Each cell describes what a pillar looks like at a given level - read across a row to plan one pillar's roadmap, or down a column to see what an organization at that level can demonstrate across all four pillars. Overlaid on the cells, the colored role icons mark the minimum level each agent type must reach on that pillar. The rightmost column states what breaks if you stay at or below a level, and those risks compound the further left you sit — the argument for investing before an incident, not after.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

How to use the matrix (3 steps). Score each pillar by finding the highest level where you meet every criterion, including all levels beneath it. Find your floor by taking the lowest of your four pillar scores — security doesn't average out, and a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. Match your floor to deployment bounds by reading across the row: any agent role whose icon sits to the right of your floor is not cleared for production deployment, and pushing past it directly triggers Excessive Agency, the #1 risk in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM and Agentic Applications.

The defaults here are a starting point, not a verdict. The pillar criteria, the weights, and the scoring logic will be published as an open source, where you can read the full methodology, score your own organization, and tweak the parameters to fit your own risk profile and constraints, rather than recalculating by hand each time something changes. 

## State of Agentic AI Security and Governance 2.01

This blog focuses on a specific section of the full OWASP guide, “[State of Agentic AI Security and Governance 2.01](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/state-of-agentic-ai-security-and-governance/)”, which expands on what this preview covers regarding agentic capability maturity and the security considerations organizations need to address.

AIMM is an assurance framework, not a vendor taxonomy or a product, and it is built around one of those four pillars rather than treating them as equals.
